clue.text: Return of work caused application to head

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word for work is read from its end

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work
made happen, brought about

explanation.surface: A piece of work sent back led to a request being put to the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Application' and 'head' suggest a job application to a manager; read literally, it is something applied to the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomade is a scented hair ointment, literally something applied to the scalp.

clue.text: Summit that is run less well

parts.note: a peak is a summit
i.e. stands for id est, that is
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A mountain-top climb that has gone badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peaky' is British slang for looking pale and unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Peaky is colloquial for slightly ill, so the comparative means more poorly, in poorer health.

clue.text: United finished the game

definitions.meaning: first meaning: paired or joined together
second meaning: won at chess by checkmate

explanation.walkthrough: 'United' looks like a football team ending its match; it is simply joined, as of a pair.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both paired up as partners and having won at chess by checkmating the opposing king.

clue.text: First half of dull game, involving king and queen and noblewoman

indicators.note: first half of asks for only the opening part of the word, its leading letters

parts.note: the first two of the four letters
a board game whose key pieces are king and queen

explanation.surface: A dull game of cards with royal pieces and a lady of rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Involving king and queen' tempts you to insert K and Q; it only describes which game is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A duchess is the wife of a duke or a woman holding a ducal title, so a high-ranking noblewoman.

clue.text: Time added to syllabus — you're not likely to take it well

definitions.text: you're not likely to take it well

parts.note: a table is a list or schedule, as a syllabus is
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Extra time is tacked onto a course syllabus, which no one is likely to take on happily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take it well' sounds like accepting news calmly; here it means you are not likely to swallow one when you are healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: A tablet is a pill, medicine generally taken only when someone is ill rather than in good health.

clue.text: Stick poster in this location

parts.note: an ad is an advertisement, such as a poster
here means at this place

explanation.surface: An instruction to put a poster up right here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' reads as a command to the bill-poster; it is the definition, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere is to cling or be fastened to something, so a synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Arrogance frequently displayed in rows with son

indicators.note: something displayed in another is shown inside it, so one piece is placed within

parts.note: lines are rows
oft is an old word for often
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A haughty attitude is often shown in arguments involving a son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rows' rhymes with cows (quarrels) in the surface but means lines here.
explanation.definitionFit: Loftiness can mean haughty pride, an air of looking down on others, which is arrogance.

clue.text: Sharpest assessment for sailor?

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
a test is an assessment

explanation.surface: The most rigorous examination a seaman could face.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads the answer as a phrase, a test for a tar; the question mark flags that split.
explanation.definitionFit: Tart means sour or acid in taste, or cutting in manner, so the superlative is a synonym.

clue.text: Flibbertigibbet sent wrong kit for naturalists

indicators.note: something that has gone wrong is out of order, so these letters are muddled

parts.note: a butterfly is a flighty, frivolous person
the letters of sent, rearranged

explanation.surface: A scatterbrained person dispatched the wrong equipment for a nature outing.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturalists collecting insects use these fine-meshed nets on handles, so they are part of the equipment.

clue.text: Monumental square crossed by tank

indicators.note: something crossed by another has that other running through its middle, so one piece sits inside

parts.note: a vat is a large tank for liquid
S is an abbreviation for square

explanation.surface: A monumental town square has a tank driving across it.
explanation.walkthrough: The S goes inside VAT, between the A and the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something of enormous size or scale, so they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Heard gunshots and became inspired

parts.note: to catch a remark is to hear it
gunfire, shots discharged

explanation.surface: Someone heard shots being fired and was moved to action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' is not a sound signal here; it simply means caught, as in catching what someone said.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch fire is, figuratively, to become excited or animated, like an idea or performer suddenly coming alive.

clue.text: Poser taken in hand by forty-niner?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a puzzling question or conundrum
second meaning: a coarse sieve, as held by a gold prospector

explanation.surface: A puzzle that a gold rusher might take on.
explanation.walkthrough: A forty-niner was a prospector in the 1849 California gold rush, who sifted gravel through a sieve to find gold.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a conundrum and a coarse sieve for separating gravel, the tool of a gold panner.

clue.text: Colonists' site developed after limited period

indicators.note: a site that is developed is built over and changed, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: a term is a fixed, limited span of time
the letters of site, rearranged

explanation.surface: Settlers' land was built upon after a short stay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colonists' suggests settlers; these colonists are insects that live in colonies.
explanation.definitionFit: These insects live in large organised colonies, building mounds, so they are colonists in a literal sense.

clue.text: Porches traditionally providing shelter for band

indicators.note: words that shelter something hold it inside them, so the answer lies within the run of letters

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Porches have long been where a band could shelter from the rain.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a large group of musicians playing together, so it is a kind of band.

clue.text: Types of publication firm endorses

parts.note: firm means hard, solid
to back is to support or endorse

explanation.surface: A company gives its approval to certain kinds of publication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a noun meaning company; it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardbacks are books bound in stiff covers, one of the formats in which books are published.

clue.text: Clear about kiss succeeding

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: to net is to clear as profit
X is the conventional sign for a kiss

explanation.surface: Someone is unambiguous about a kiss being a success.
explanation.definitionFit: Next means following straight after, which is what succeeding means in sequence.

clue.text: Put on alert by the sound of it …

indicators.note: the phrase asks us to judge by how a word is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: to warn is to alert, and in British speech the two words sound alike

explanation.surface: Someone is put on alert, apparently, and the ellipsis carries the sentence on to the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British pronunciation warn and the answer are identical in sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes that have been put on are worn, so the past participles match.

clue.text: Marry nurses at church under close scrutiny

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold something close and cradle it, so one piece holds the others inside

parts.note: to wed is to marry
taken as written
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A wedding conducted in church is closely observed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' looks like hospital staff, but it is a verb meaning holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Something watched is observed carefully, kept under surveillance, which is close scrutiny.

clue.text: … by a seemingly slow team

parts.note: taken as written
something long seems to take a slow age
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: alerted by a team that looks sluggish.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this to 16 across for the surface only; each clue is solved on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Beside and next to are what by means in 'stand by the door', exactly the sense of this preposition.

clue.text: Man lion mauled of little worth

indicators.note: something mauled is torn about and mangled, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man attacked by a lion is not worth much afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominal sum is token, tiny and insignificant, as in a nominal fee.

clue.text: Ladder's central components substituted

indicators.note: central components are the letters in the middle of the word, the ones at its heart

parts.note: the two middle letters of ladder are D and D, a pair of Ds

explanation.surface: The middle rungs of a ladder have been replaced.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle of ladder is DD, which is read out as 'double D'.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor who doubles for another stands in for them, so doubled means substituted.

clue.text: Look into predator's northbound trail

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading from bottom to top, backwards
into means going inside, so the first word is put within the second

parts.note: a wolf is a predator
lo is an old word meaning look

explanation.surface: Someone investigates the track a predator took heading north.
explanation.definitionFit: To trail someone is to follow them, tracking their path, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Burton's beast originally kicked like a mule

indicators.note: kicked about means knocked out of order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

indicators.note: originally points to the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: the first letter of beast

explanation.surface: Richard Burton's animal lashed out the way a mule does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kicked like a mule' reads as one phrase, but 'kicked' is the anagram signal and 'like a mule' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Mules are proverbially obstinate, so behaving like one means being obstinate and unyielding.

clue.text: Second protest abruptly closed temple

indicators.note: something closed abruptly is cut off before its natural end, so the word loses its final letters

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second
to squeal is to complain loudly

explanation.surface: A second demonstration led to a temple being shut without warning.
explanation.walkthrough: The protest word is clipped of its last two letters before joining MO.
explanation.definitionFit: A mosque is a Muslim place of worship, and temple is used loosely for any such building.

clue.text: Aerosol, eg with extremely poor contents

indicators.note: contents are what something holds inside, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: say means for example, as eg does

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes, the first and last letters of the word

parts.note: the first and last letters of poor

explanation.surface: An aerosol can, for example, with very poor contents inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerosol is a canister releasing a fine mist, so a spray is the thing or product it delivers.

clue.text: Explorer's rough hut revealed

parts.note: a shack is a crude hut
let on means revealed a secret

explanation.surface: A polar explorer's crude hut was uncovered.
explanation.walkthrough: Ernest Shackleton led Antarctic expeditions; his huts there still survive.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Ernest Shackleton was a celebrated Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer, so he is an example of the category.

clue.text: Bank just ignores me

indicators.note: what is ignored is left out, so those letters are dropped from the word

parts.note: merely means only, just
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: A bank simply pays me no attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks like a noun for a financial institution, but it is the verb, as in 'bank on'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bank on someone is to depend on them, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Refuse to acknowledge one's wearing blue

indicators.note: a word that is wearing another has that other on it, wrapped around, so one goes inside

parts.note: feeling blue is feeling down
one is I, and 's stands for is

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to admit they are dressed in blue.
explanation.definitionFit: To disown a person or thing is to deny any connection with it, to refuse to recognise it.

clue.text: Before deplorable delay Penny was in the game

indicators.note: something deplorable is in a bad state, so these letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for penny
the letters of delay, rearranged

explanation.surface: Before a terrible hold-up, Penny took part in the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny' reads as a woman's name, but it is just the coin abbreviation; 'Before' places it ahead of the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To have played is to have taken part in a match or sport, been on the field.
